rationale: The child question's remaining counterevidence was that a partition landing while a follower was already campaigning is not covered by the twelve trials, which left the consequence bounded by measurement rather than by the mechanism. Reading the two paths that gate these events answers it from the source: a follower that has a known leader rejects vote requests before it even compares terms, so a candidate only becomes electable on that node once the node's own heartbeat timer has expired, and that timer is reset by each heartbeat from the same leader whose lease is running down; ValidateConfig enforces the relation that makes the leader's lease the earlier of the two on any node that shares its settings. This submission records that answer as a source-only revision of the child account, narrows the consequence to uniform configurations, and names the mixed-timing exception the API permits but this run did not construct.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only revision that closes the phase limitation of the previous account; the twelve-trial receipt and its operands are unchanged and remain the measured basis. The question was whether a partition landing while a follower is already campaigning could put a competing leader in place before the cut-off leader's confirmations stop. Two gates in the follower path answer it. First, a node that knows a leader refuses a vote request from any other candidate before it looks at terms at all, so a pre-existing candidate cannot collect the vote of a peer that still has the leader in view, and that peer only clears its view and starts its own campaign when its heartbeat timer fires, having been reset by the same leader whose lease is expiring. Second, ValidateConfig enforces LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout per node, so for a cluster that shares its settings the cut-off leader's lease expires no later than the earliest moment any peer can begin campaigning, and the peer then also needs a full election round before a new leader exists. That is the same ordering the twelve trials measured (last confirmations 44-49ms, competing leaders 67-142ms) and it explains it mechanically rather than falling out of scheduling: the confirmation window closes first because the leader's own lease check is the earliest event in the sequence, and the leader's lease check counts voters only, which is why the reachable nonvoter prolongs confirmation without prolonging leadership. The consequence of the parent finding is therefore bounded for uniform configurations, and the unsound confirmation remains the surviving defect. The exception is a cluster whose nodes do not share settings: a follower configured with a heartbeat timeout shorter than the leader's leader-lease timeout could begin an election first, and the relation is enforced per node rather than across the cluster. Nothing in the captured defaults produces that, a mixed configuration is what would, and this run did not construct one.
counterevidence: The mixed-timing exception is not merely theoretical to the extent that rollouts leave nodes with different settings and the library validates each node independently; it is unmeasured here, and it is the one configuration in which the confirmation window and a competing leader could overlap.

The gating argument assumes peers evaluate the vote request as recorded in the snapshot's requestVote path, including the transfer-flagged bypass; a transfer-derived request waives the known-leader gate, which is the mechanism examined and refuted in the sibling question for internal producers.
No application read is served in these runs, so even an overlap would only be a missing basis for a consistent read rather than an observed stale result.
limitations: This revision is a source argument appended to a measured account; it does not add an execution, and the twelve-trial receipt remains the observed evidence.
The mixed-timing case is identified rather than tested; constructing it would need per-node configurations, which the cluster helper used here does not provide.
The reasoning covers the two gates named above and not every possible way a candidate could gain a vote, for example a peer that has never heard of the leader because it joined afterwards.
